newsitem.title: UK: Bloody Sunday relatives mourn for justice.
newsitem.headline: Bloody Sunday relatives mourn for justice.

text.p: Relatives of 13 Catholics killed by British troops on "Bloody Sunday" 25 years ago honoured their dead on Thursday and vowed to keep campaigning for an apology from the British government.

Bells rang out and a two-minute silence fell on a group of several hundred mourners around a simple grey monument which marks one of the most emotive days in the calendar of Northern Ireland's pro-Irish 40 percent Catholic minority.
John Kelly, whose teenage brother was killed said: "The campaign to clear their names will continue."
But British Prime Minister John Major told parliament, "Without fresh evidence, I see no advantage in raking over these old problems. With fresh evidence...we would examine it."

Kelly said the British government "lied through its teeth" about the incident in which paratroopers fired on an unarmed Catholic crowd and helped swell the Irish Republican Army (IRA), the guerrilla group fighting British rule.
"But we are determined that the truth will out and hopefully our loved ones will rest in peace and those who are grieving will some day have comfort," Kelly told Reuters.
The campaign received reinforcement from an Irish legal expert who said some of the British paratroopers involved in the 1972 killings should have been prosecuted for murder.
Dermot Walsh, a law professor at Limerick University, told Reuters there were discrepancies in statements made by the soldiers to a British enquiry into the killings.
Britain released the statements last year under pressure from victims' relatives and a human rights group, he said.
"There are grounds for preferring charges of murder or attempted murder against some of the soldiers on the basis of some of their original statements," he said.
Walsh was speaking ahead of publication in Londonderry of his critical study of the official report by Lord Widgery, who was then Britain's chief justice.
"The Widgery findings are fatally flawed because they are based substantially on unreliable evidence," he said.
Widgery said troops had been shot at and some of the dead may have handled guns or explosives before they were hit.
Northern Ireland's minority Catholics regard the report as a "whitewash" of what they say were unprovoked killings at an Irish nationalist rally.
No soldiers were hurt and no weapons were found at the scene of the killings, in the heart of Londonderry's Bogside district.
Walsh examined papers, including soldiers' "original statements", which he said conflicted materially with evidence they gave to the Widgery tribunal.
"These new documents...contain original statements that soldiers gave on the night of Bloody Sunday to military police, and...other things such as memos," he said.
It was disturbing, he said, that "the soldiers' original statements were available to counsel for the tribunal and Lord Widgery but not counsel for the deceased".
"The whole report was seriously infected by the appearance of a bias to the extent that it undermined its whole legality," the Irish professor said.
"Most disturbing of all is the fact that (the documents) portray Lord Widgery himself as being prepared to play down evidence favourable to the deceased and amplify evidence favourable to the Army."
